personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Alicia is a consistent supporting presence on the Gryffindor Quidditch team across multiple years. Her personality is characterized by warmth and team loyalty, but also by emotional expressiveness and a willingness to speak up. She reacts with sharp moral indignation when provoked: she shrieks 'How dare you!' at Malfoy's use of 'Mudblood' (Book Scene 10), protests injustice with feeling ('It's just so unfair' and 'And banning Fred when he didn't even do anything!' in Book Scenes 90–93), and expresses anxiety after Harry's fall ('We thought you'd died,' she said, who was shaking — Book Scene 22). She also has a soothing, team-steadying side: 'Stop worrying, Oliver, we don't mind a bit of rain' (Book Scene 20), and practical utility in mundane team logistics ('Andrew Kirke and Jack Sloper. Neither of them are brilliant…' Book Scene 100). She participates in the team's social life — laughing at Fred and George's jokes (Book Scene 31), chatting with Angelina by the fire (Book Scene 49), offering comfort about Katie's injury (Book Scene 105). Her voice is not distinctive in syntax or register, but she is emotionally engaged, morally vocal, and socially grounded.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: In the film corpus (Chamber of Secrets screenplay), Alicia is listed by name in a stage direction as one of the Gryffindor Quidditch team members trailing Oliver Wood (Film Scene 1 / screenplay Scene 45). She is present as a named background figure. She has no dialogue, no observable emotional reactions, no moral speech, and no individually attributed actions. The Mudblood confrontation scene is present in the film and the team is present, but Alicia's specific reaction — her shriek of 'How dare you!' — is not attributed to her; Fred and George charge Malfoy and are held back by Wood, and Ron attempts the curse. The film corpus provided does not include Prisoner of Azkaban, Goblet of Fire, or Order of the Phoenix screenplay material, which is where the bulk of Alicia's book personality is displayed.
personality_voice.difference: The film corpus available provides only one scene where Alicia is present: she is named in a stage direction as part of the Quidditch team group. No dialogue, no individual emotional reaction, no moral outburst is attributed to her in the available film material. Her most defining personality expressions from the books — her indignant 'How dare you!', her grief and shaking after Harry's fall, her furious reactions to the Umbridge-era injustices, her comforting and soothing interventions — are entirely absent from the film corpus provided. However, the corpus is extremely limited to Chamber of Secrets only, and the absence of Order of the Phoenix and Prisoner of Azkaban screenplay material means the corpus cannot confirm whether these traits were or were not preserved in later films.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: A penalty is warranted because the only film evidence available reduces Alicia to an unnamed background figure with no voice. Her most important personality moments — specifically the 'How dare you!' reaction (which is directly in the same scene that does appear in the film) — are not preserved in the film corpus. The Mudblood confrontation scene in the film assigns emotional reactions exclusively to Fred, George, and Ron; Alicia's individual outrage is absorbed into the group reaction. However, the corpus limitation means this penalty cannot be fully confirmed across the whole film run. Score placed in the 14–17 range: character remains recognizable as a Quidditch Chaser with team loyalty, but important personality expressions and her distinct voice are reduced or absent.
personality_voice.evidence_status: Directly evidenced (book baseline); Directly evidenced (film corpus limited to one scene with no Alicia dialogue or individual reaction)

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Alicia's narrative role in the books is as an active Chaser who functions within the Quidditch team ensemble. Her agency is modest but specific: she takes penalty shots (Book Scenes 37–38, 45), scores goals (Book Scene 43), reacts individually to injustice (Book Scene 10 — 'How dare you!'), voices team concerns to Oliver (Book Scene 11 — 'Oliver, this is insane'), provides practical information (Book Scene 100 — names the replacement Beaters), asks about Katie Bell (Book Scene 60–61), participates in the DA (Book Scene 67, 70), and appears at the Battle of Hogwarts (Book Scene 107). She is not a plot driver, but she regularly initiates small acts: speaking up, asking questions, comforting, informing. She is not purely decorative.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: In the available film corpus, Alicia appears only in a stage direction as part of the Quidditch team group. No individual action, line, decision, or initiative is attributed to her. The scene in which she could have spoken up — the Mudblood confrontation — is present in the film, but her individual contribution ('How dare you!') is not preserved. Her agency in Quidditch play, her DA participation, her injury by Bletchley, and her team-steadying interventions are all outside the available film corpus.
narrative_role_agency.difference: In the one scene where both book and film corpus overlap (the Mudblood confrontation), Alicia's specific act of agency — her outraged verbal response — is absent from the film, absorbed into the group reaction. All other agency from the books (scoring, speaking up to Wood, naming replacements, attending DA) is simply not represented in the available film corpus. The corpus covers too small a portion of the films to confirm how much agency she retains or loses across the full series.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: A moderate penalty is applied because the one directly comparable scene (Mudblood confrontation) removes her individual act of agency and replaces it with a group reaction. The remaining agency losses cannot be confirmed from the available corpus. Score placed in the 10–13 range: role and agency are clearly altered in the available evidence, though limited corpus prevents full assessment.
narrative_role_agency.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for the Mudblood scene comparison; Not enough evidence for the full range of Alicia's agency across films

There is no deep internal conflict — she is not a character defined by moral ambiguity or contradictory desires. Her motivation is essentially team loyalty and a moral compass that reacts against prejudice and unfair treatment.

She ages from a fourth-year reserve (Book 1) to a graduating seventh-year (Book 5/6), but no arc of growth, change, or resolution is established for her individually.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Alicia's key relationships in the books are: (1) the Gryffindor Quidditch team ensemble, especially Angelina Johnson (they are consistently paired — chatting together, reacting together, named together throughout the books), and (2) a minor but consistent relationship with Harry as teammate. Her dynamic with Angelina is one of close friendship and social solidarity. Her relationship with the team is defined by warmth, shared purpose, and mutual support. She is also part of the broader DA group. No romantic or deeply individualized relationship is developed.

The film presents the group, not the individual relationships within it.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: A moderate penalty for the loss of the Angelina–Alicia friendship texture, which is the most individually defining relationship Alicia has in the books. However, the books give her specific moments that add texture: her individual moral outrage at 'Mudblood' (distinguishing her from the group); her anxiety and shaking after Harry's fall; her furious reaction to Umbridge's bans and Fred's unjust punishment; her soothing reassurance to Oliver; her being jinxed by Bletchley in the library (an incident that reveals both Snape's bias and her vulnerability as a target); her practical assessment of the replacement Beaters; her attendance at the DA and the Battle of Hogwarts. These moments, taken together, produce a character with a specific moral voice, emotional range, and narrative utility beyond simple decoration.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The film corpus reduces Alicia to a name in a stage direction. None of the specific moments listed above are present in the available film material. Her individual moral outrage in the Mudblood scene is absorbed into the group. Her Bletchley jinx, her DA involvement, her Battle of Hogwarts presence, her soothing of Oliver, her shaking after Harry's fall — none of these appear in the film corpus provided.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: Essentially all of the book material that gives Alicia individual texture is absent from the film corpus. Whether this is due to the corpus being limited to Chamber of Secrets only, or because the films genuinely removed this material in later installments, cannot be fully determined. However, the one scene where book and film corpus directly overlap (the Mudblood confrontation) confirms that the film removed her individual contribution.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: A noticeable simplification is confirmed by the available evidence. The only directly comparable scene eliminates her individual voice. The broader absence of all textured moments cannot be attributed solely to corpus limitations, since later films (PoA, GoF, OotP) are known to keep Alicia as a background figure without individual dialogue in most cases. Score: 9 — noticeable simplification with important nuances missing, though the character's ensemble function is structurally preserved.
